vignette:
James, a 47-year-old bus driver from a small town in North America, begins his story on a rainy evening that seems to haunt him, no matter the weather outside. He has a routine—every day, he drives the same route, navigating familiar streets, passing the same landmarks. But that particular night, a simple drive turned into a nightmare.

As James recalls that fateful evening, he feels the weight in his chest. He can’t escape the image of the police car that suddenly veered into his lane, colliding with his bus. The sound of metal crunching, the shattering of glass, the cries of passengers—it all floods back to him like an unwelcome specter. He remembers the chaos as first responders rushed to the scene, the flashing lights illuminating the darkness, and the feeling of helplessness that enveloped him as he sat stunned in his seat, unable to process what had just occurred.

In the weeks that follow the accident, James finds himself grappling with an overwhelming sense of anxiety that he can’t shake. He returns to work, trying to push through the memories that cling to him, but every time he gets behind the wheel, the sound of the crash echoes in his mind. He can't help but replay the events, questioning if he could have done something differently. His once comforting routine transforms into a source of dread. He notices the way his hands tremble on the steering wheel, how his heart races when he sees flashing lights in his rearview mirror, even when they belong to a distant vehicle. 

At night, the memories invade his sleep. He wakes up drenched in sweat, heart pounding, the echo of sirens ringing in his ears. The sensation of being trapped in that bus, unable to escape the chaos, grips him tightly. He becomes increasingly isolated, preferring the solace of his small apartment to social gatherings or even simple conversations with friends. The vibrant conversations that once filled his life fade away, replaced by a heavy silence that he finds strangely comforting.

As weeks turn into months, James struggles to maintain the façade of normalcy at work. He engages in the motions of his job but is often lost in thought, his mind wandering to the accident. His colleagues notice his withdrawal but don’t press him; they know he’s always been the quiet type, but now his silence feels heavier, more profound. He feels like a ghost, floating through the motions of life, disconnected from the world around him.

James begins to experience physical symptoms as well—tightness in his chest, chronic headaches, and an overwhelming fatigue that seems to sap his strength. He thinks about seeking help but hesitates, feeling ashamed of his struggle. He tells himself he should be grateful—after all, he survived the accident. But gratitude feels hollow when he’s consumed by fear and anxiety. He worries he’ll never be the same, never regain the sense of safety that once came so easily.

During one particularly difficult shift, a sudden loud noise—a motorcycle backfiring—sends him spiraling. He grips the steering wheel tightly, heart racing, as the world around him blurs. He feels the urge to jump out of the bus, to escape, to run away from the memories that threaten to engulf him. His breath quickens, and he has to pull over, tears stinging his eyes as he fights to get control of himself. He sits there for what feels like an eternity, trying to calm the storm inside him, wishing for the peace he once took for granted.

As he navigates his days, James finds himself increasingly drawn to the idea of speaking to someone about his experience. A flicker of hope ignites within him, a desire to reclaim his life and his passion for driving. He contemplates reaching out for help, contemplating how to voice the pain that has taken root deep within him. For now, he remains a bus driver behind the wheel, but he knows that he is also a man in search of healing, yearning to find his way back to the surface.
